t: Section 1853(a)(1)(C) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1395w–23(a)(1)(C)) is amended by adding at the end the following new clause:“(iii) Application of coding intensity adjustment for 2011 and subsequent years.—“(I) Requirement to apply in 2011 through 2013.—In order to ensure payment accuracy, the Secretary shall conduct an analysis of the differences described in clause (ii)(I). The Secretary shall ensure that the results of such analysis are incorporated into the risk scores for 2011, 2012, and 2013.“(II) Authority to apply in 2014 and subsequent years.—The Secretary may, as appropriate, incorporate the results of such analysis into the risk scores for 2014 and subsequent years.”.

fable.w: The section directs the Secretary to conduct an internal analysis of coding differences and to incorporate the results into Medicare Advantage risk scores. The tempting reading is that adjusting payment risk scores implies rulemaking or stakeholder input, but the text requires no regulation, comment period, hearing, advisory body, or consultation with any party outside the federal government. Every actor involved is inside the federal government, so this is not participation.
fable.s: the Secretary shall conduct an analysis of the differences described in clause (ii)(I). The Secretary shall ensure that the results of such analysis are incorporated into the risk scores for 2011, 2012, and 2013.

opus.w: The section only directs the Secretary to run an internal analysis and fold the results into Medicare Advantage risk scores. It names no states, experts, companies or members of the public, and it calls for no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking or right to sue. The tempting reading treats risk-score changes as a rulemaking that invites outside comment, but this text grants no regulatory authority and requires no outside input. The decision stays entirely inside the federal government.
opus.s: In order to ensure payment accuracy, the Secretary shall conduct an analysis of the differences described in clause (ii)(I). The Secretary shall ensure that the results of such analysis are incorporated into the risk scores for 2011, 2012, and 2013.
opus.b:
I'd label this **No**: the section involves no one outside the federal government.

1. **The tempting reading.** Medicare Advantage risk-score adjustments do affect outside parties. In practice, CMS also announces payment changes through an advance notice that invites comments. It's tempting to treat this as a rulemaking-type decision with outside input.
2. **Why that fails.** The text itself never mentions rulemaking, regulations, comments, hearings or consulting anyone. The Secretary alone runs the analysis and applies the results to the risk scores. A practice that exists elsewhere, but isn't in this text, doesn't count.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary to conduct an internal analysis and incorporate its results into risk scores. It does not mandate consultation, coordination, or input from any party outside the federal government (such as states, tribes, the public, or independent experts). The actors involved are solely federal officials (the Secretary). Therefore, it does not meet the definition of participation.
qwen_chat.s: the Secretary shall conduct an analysis of the differences described in clause (ii)(I). The Secretary shall ensure that the results of such analysis are incorporated into the risk scores for 2011, 2012, and 2013.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "analysis" implies consulting with outside experts or data providers, thus constituting participation. However, the text does not specify *who* conducts the analysis or *with whom* the Secretary consults. It simply mandates an internal administrative action (conducting an analysis) by the Secretary. Without explicit mention of outside parties (states, tribes, public, independent experts, etc.), this is an internal agency process.
